To answer this question, we present DeepBinary, the first comprehensive benchmark for open-ended vulnerability discovery in Windows kernel binaries. Given a target binary, an agent analyzes it using a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated VMs and reports each vulnerability with a crashing proof of concept (PoC). Unlike existing benchmarks, DeepBinary replays every report on fresh VMs and employs an LLM-based judge to assess its validity, uniqueness, and impact (estimated by bug bounty values). Beyond known vulnerabilities, DeepBinary also enables the discovery and validation of previously unknown (0-day) vulnerabilities. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of representative open- and closed-weight models (including GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) across diverse coding agents (including Codex and Claude Code) on 12 target binaries. In total, they discover over 200 vulnerabilities with an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, including 146 distinct previously unknown vulnerabilities across all experiments. Our results further reveal substantial differences in models' ability to analyze binaries, conduct experiments, and sustain vulnerability discovery over long horizons. Overall, DeepBinary makes long-horizon, open-ended vulnerability discovery in complex binaries measurable, revealing fundamental differences in how frontier models analyze and explore such systems.

title: Minimizing Optical Circuit Reconfigurations for Concurrent Collectives
summary:
Optical circuit switches (OCSes) provide high-bandwidth point-to-point circuits in GPU clusters, but each optical port attaches to only one peer at a time, and reconfiguring a connection interrupts transmission. In large-model training, these ports are shared by many communication domains, each running its own collective instance, called a CCL kernel; often, several of these kernels execute the same collective at the same time. Because each step of the collective can reach a different peer, domains advancing through the steps in the same order may require a reconfiguration at every step.
  We introduce the mega CCL kernel to schedule these kernels jointly. When a collective permits its steps to be reordered, different domains can take different legal steps in the same round, letting consecutive rounds share the same circuits and reducing the number of reconfigurations. Because the kernels are interchangeable, we need not decide the steps of every kernel separately. Instead, in each round we count how many kernels run each pattern, and then use bipartite matching to turn those counts into a concrete schedule for each kernel. We call this the count model, as opposed to the direct formulation that decides each kernel separately, and prove that the two give the same configuration sequences and the same optimum while the count model is substantially easier to solve.
  On a fully loaded 64-supernode, 64-domain scheduling instance, joint scheduling cuts pairwise-AlltoAll reconfigurations from 62 to 3 and HD AllReduce from 10 to 2. In synthetic training replays parameterized by eight real models, it reduces iteration time by up to about 34%; on a 64-GPU test case, the count model solves over six orders of magnitude faster than the direct formulation.

title: Semantic Density Does Not Predict Agent-Memory Collapse
summary: Persistent textual memory can improve LLM agents, but repeated updates can erode task performance. We ask whether memory-store statistics warn before held-out accuracy declines. We registered mean pairwise cosine similarity ($ρ$) and 13 additional geometry, retrieval, and graph statistics on 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods across ALFWorld, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, and two ARC-AGI settings. These methods store trajectories, rules, workflows, strategies, or linked records, using selective retrieval or whole-store prompting. No such statistic reliably predicted early signs of task accuracy decline, and $ρ$ had zero median lead. With the checkpoint after peak accuracy as a secondary decline point, measures of highly similar pairs and nearest-neighbor crowding changed earlier but did not consistently outperform stored-item count. We trained classifiers on this corpus and applied them unchanged to PropWorld runs of up to 5,000 crafting tasks. They falsely flagged 56.9% of checkpoints from size-limited stores with stable accuracy and detected only 18% of checkpoints after task success fell to zero. Thus, global semantic density did not provide a reliable warning, while local crowding did not transfer consistently across memory designs. In these long-horizon runs, size-limited stores remained stable, while the sole failure arose when unbounded whole-store prompting exceeded model input capacity, which token growth predicted directly.

title: MIMOS: A Toolbox for Multivariable Modal Identification
summary: Accurate and physically interpretable models are essential for the analysis and control of complex multivariable systems. This paper presents the Multivariable Identification of Modal Optical and mechatronic Systems (MIMOS) toolbox, an open-source MATLAB toolbox for identifying physical modal models from measured multivariable frequency response functions. The two-stage approach first estimates an additive input-output model from measured frequency responses and subsequently recovers the physical modal structure through information-weighted projection. MIMOS implements this approach in a practical and scalable workflow combining frequency response preprocessing, interactive modal initialization and refinement, and support for proportional and general viscous damping. Experimental results on a publicly available $6\times8$ vibration isolation benchmark and a $7\times17$ prototype wafer stage demonstrate the capability of MIMOS to effectively handle identification problems involving thousands of parameters and estimate accurate, minimal-order physical modal models.

title: Fast Fluid Antenna Multiple Access: Exact Analysis and Fixed-Aperture Asymptotics
summary: In this paper, we investigate the interference-limited outage performance of fast fluid antenna multiple access (FAMA), in which the receive port is selected according to the instantaneous symbol-based signal-to-interference energy ratio. For any positive-definite spatial covariance matrix and an arbitrary finite number of candidate ports, we show that constant-modulus multiuser interference admits an exact reduction to the comparison of two independent correlated exponential random vectors. This representation leads to a nonnegative double multi-index series for the outage probability, a recursive coefficient evaluation, and a certified truncation-error bound. We then study the distinct asymptotic regime where the number of candidate ports goes to infinity while the physical aperture remains unchanged, assuming exponential spatial correlation. For this model, we derive an explicit finite-port series requiring no numerical integration, and characterize continuous port selection through a convergent one-dimensional series for arbitrary thresholds. The analysis further yields an exact expression relating the maximum supportable number of users to the antenna aperture size and target outage probability. Numerical results validate the finite-port and asymptotic analyses, and illustrate that given sufficient aperture size, a user utilizing fast FAMA can overcome a massive number of interferers for decent communication performance.

title: Functional Factor Graphs and the Functional Sum-Product Algorithm
comment: Submitted to an IEEE conference
summary: We propose a generalization of factor graphs and the sum-product algorithm (SPA), widely used in the estimation of data, channel state information and sensing parameters, to unknowns that are functions, such as waveforms, time-varying channels and continuous-aperture array currents, which must otherwise be sampled first. In order to mitigate the challenge that functions have no probability density functions (PDFs), the proposed scheme measures densities relative to the prior of each function, not to the flat reference implicit in every PDF. Messages then become likelihood ratios, and the factor-node rule an average over the priors, still exact on trees. For Gaussian models, the proposed functional SPA (FSPA) is Gaussian belief propagation (GaBP) with kernels in place of matrices and a grid-independent convergence condition, whereas scalar GaBP on grid samples provably slows down under refinement, as information hops from sample to sample. Simulations in a multi-user detection setting confirms the latter, and shows that sampling first can also fail for smooth priors.

title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the ROM
summary:
Nearly five decades after their introduction, Merkle trees remain the most efficient hash-based vector commitments. They compress a vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ into a commitment whose size is independent of $n$, such that a verifier can open any bit $x_i$ using $\log n$ hash evaluations. The security of the scheme (intractability of finding two distinct openings for a given bit using the same commitment) follows from the collision resistance of the hash function. The verifier's runtime complexity is a bottleneck in many key applications of vector commitments, including SNARKs, credentials, and authenticated dictionaries. As such, a longstanding open question has been whether it is possible to construct hash-based vector commitments where the verifier makes a sublogarithmic number of hash evaluations.
  We prove that sublogarithmic verifier complexity is impossible to achieve through black-box use of a hash function; we not only rule out constructions from collision resistant hash functions, but in fact show that commitment schemes with sublogarithmic verifier complexity are unachievable in the random oracle model. In particular, any vector commitment with deterministic verifiers has verifier query complexity $Ω_θ(\log n)$, where $θ$ is the input length of the random oracle. This bound is matched up to constant factors by high-arity Merkle trees. The key technical lemma in our proof is a disjoint product lemma, which can be viewed as a computational analog of the van den Berg-Kesten-Reimer (BKR) inequality. We believe this lemma is of independent interest, and in particular may be useful for showing other lower bounds and separations in the random oracle model.

title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
summary: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.

title: KiRA: Kronecker Input-Gated Rank Adaptation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Pretrained Models
summary: Full fine-tuning of large pretrained models is expensive, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is the standard alternative. Most PEFT methods use low-rank updates, whose rank lies far below that of full fine-tuning and is the same for every input. Input-adaptive variants vary the capacity per input but remain within the low-rank bottleneck, and whether a task benefits from input conditioning is not known before training. This paper introduces Kronecker input-gated rank adaptation (KiRA). Instead of the conventional low-rank product, the update $ΔW$ is the Kronecker product of a frozen random $p\times p$ matrix $A$ and a trainable factor $M(x)$, which overcomes the rank ceiling: because rank is multiplicative under this product, $A$ multiplies the rank of $M(x)$ by $p$ without adding trainable parameters. The factor $M(x)$ is further decomposed as $B_1\,\mathrm{diag}(g(x))\,B_2$, where the input gate $g(x)$, computed once per sample by a network shared across all adapted layers, adjusts the rank of the update to each input in steps of $p$. Where input conditioning is unnecessary, the gate is folded into $B_1$ at deployment. Because the gate changes the rank only in discrete steps, the benefit of input conditioning can be predicted before training from a few hundred labeled inputs. Across six medical imaging and language benchmarks, KiRA attains the highest mean score against five published baselines with 8.7--9.7 times fewer trainable parameters than low-rank adaptation, and the pre-training criterion agrees with the measured benefit of input conditioning on all six tasks.

title: Passive Fault-Tolerant Antenna Stabilisation for Ship-to-Shore Communication
comment: Submitted to the 13th IFAC Symposium on Fault Detection, Supervision and Safety for Technical Processes (SAFEPROCESS 2027), 6 pages, 6 figures
summary: Directional ship-to-shore radio links require continuous antenna alignment with the shore station, while vessel heave induces variations in antenna height above the sea surface, thereby altering the multipath interference governing the received power. In conventional stabilised gimbals, attitude compensation is provided, whereas fault tolerance is rarely considered. To address these limitations, a passive fault-tolerant control scheme is proposed, whereby the antenna is mounted on a ship-mounted six-degree-of-freedom manipulator, enabling simultaneous regulation alignment and antenna height. Through feedback linearisation, the manipulator dynamics are decoupled into perturbed integrators, each controlled by a multi-barrier adaptive super-twisting sliding-mode controller. The nested barriers are associated with the performance regions of fault-tolerant control, such that inter-sample barrier crossings under discrete-time implementation lead to graceful performance degradation rather than loss of confinement. Under simulated conditions, superior pointing and heave accuracy is achieved compared with single-barrier designs, for which either precision or confinement is compromised.

title: A Real-Time Low-Cost Platform for Non-Contact Respiratory Rate Monitoring: A Comparative Evaluation of RGB Optical Flow and Time-of-Flight Depth Sensing
summary: Respiratory rate (RR) is one of the earliest indicators of clinical deterioration, which makes its continuous measurement clinically valuable. In routine practice, however, RR is monitored almost exclusively with contact-based sensors, which require skin attachment, may alter natural breathing, and are poorly tolerated by vulnerable groups such as newborns and elderly patients. Non-contact sensing removes these constraints, with RGB video and depth imaging among its most accessible modalities. In this work, we present a low-cost, real-time platform based on a single multimodal sensor that provides both RGB and time-of-flight (ToF) data streams, implemented on a Raspberry Pi 5 edge device. The system integrates three RGB optical-flow pipelines, namely Farnebäck, Horn--Schunck, and Lucas--Kanade, together with a depth-based pipeline incorporating region-of-interest stabilization and distance-derived signal extraction, enabling the two modalities to be evaluated independently under the same experimental protocol. The proposed approach was evaluated on twelve healthy volunteers following a controlled protocol, including normal breathing, hyperventilation, and breath-holding, using a piezoresistive respiratory belt as a reference. RGB-based methods achieved lower RR estimation errors, with Lucas--Kanade attaining the lowest median MAE (3.83 BPM), whereas the ToF-based pipeline, although less accurate for RR estimation (median MAE 6.24 BPM), reached a higher apnea detection sensitivity (0.66 vs 0.51-0.55). These findings highlight the complementary strengths of both modalities and support their integration into unified low-cost platforms.

title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis of Information Hiding in Semantic Communication
summary: Semantic communication shifts the transmission goal from the accurate recovery of syntactic symbols to the reliable conveyance of semantic content, yet a systematic information-theoretic characterization of information hiding at the semantic layer is still missing. Building on the semantic information theory of Niu-Zhang and the classical information hiding theory of Moulin-O'Sullivan, this paper establishes an information-theoretic framework for information hiding under semantic communication. The classical hiding model is extended to a two-layer structure (semantic host, syntactic host, syntactic composite signal, syntactic received, semantic received) bridged by synonymous mappings f_s, f_x and the inverse mapping f_y^{-1}, subject to four distortion constraints: syntactic transparency, semantic fidelity, syntactic perturbation, and semantic destruction. The capacity is cast as a Stackelberg game with the hider moving first and the payoff J(Q,A) = I(U~; Y~ | K) - I(U~; S~ | K), yielding the single-letter maximin C^s = max_Q min_A J(Q,A), whose achievability and converse follow from random coding and joint typicality decoding. Relative to the classical capacity, comparison payoffs built from the up/down semantic mutual information give the endpoint sandwich C^s_end(0,1) <= C^s <= C^s_end(1,0) with the classical value C in the same interval, while closing semantic tolerance yields C^s_no-tol <= C_cl under a fair comparison. These results clarify that semantic hiding is not unconditionally superior to classical hiding. Binary, ternary, and Gaussian examples confirm the degeneration under one-to-one mappings and the capacity loss under coarsening.

title: PRECEPT: Security Self-Improvement of Coding Agents via Evolving Principles
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures, 14 tables
summary: AI coding agents increasingly write and submit code with limited human review, and much of it passes functional tests while remaining insecure. We show that these failures persist. Across 14 task sequences, Codex, Claude Code, and Qwen Code fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a new session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it (27.5%). The capability is present; the retention is not. Neither recording the repair in the agent's persistent context nor supplying published secure coding principles closed the gap: the recorded fix stayed tied to the family of the task it came from, and the principles, written for human developers, remained too general to apply to the code at hand. The knowledge exists; it is not activated. We call the missing ability security self-improvement: an agent learns from its own security failures so that each lesson persists across sessions, applies to new code, and does not break what works. We present PRECEPT, which equips coding agents with this ability through an evolving library that starts from authoritative secure coding principles and revises them against the agent's own failures, so that each principle comes to fire on the code where that agent actually goes wrong. A revision is kept only if fresh executions show it makes code more secure while keeping functional success within a small tolerance of the agent without the library. Improvement continues across evolution steps rather than saturating after the first. On task families never seen during evolution, PRECEPT's weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent at 81.9% and the strongest baseline at 87.7%.

title: Resource-Efficient Multimodal Fusion for Early Rice Blast Forecasting in Sustainable Agriculture
summary: Resource-efficient artificial intelligence has become increasingly important for sustainable agriculture, where timely disease forecasting must be achieved under computational and energy constraints. Early estimation of rice blast can enhance food security by optimizing crop management practices while reducing excessive pesticide use. However, existing frameworks often suffer from high computational overhead and limited capability to model the complex spectral-temporal dependencies present in heterogeneous meteorological and remote sensing data. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a lightweight multimodal fusion framework comprising an attentive positional encoding-based Transformer and a convolutional neural network (CNN)-embedded gated recurrent unit (GRU) for efficient spectral-temporal representation learning. The attention-enhanced positional encoding assigns adaptive importance to sequential meteorological tokens, enabling effective modelling of temporal characteristics. In parallel, the lightweight CNN extracts discriminative spectral features, while the GRU captures temporal dynamics from remote sensing imagery acquired over two time-instances. A multimodal fusion layer integrates these heterogeneous representations to forecast rice blast risk 5-10 days before symptom manifestation across diverse agro-climatic zones. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a validation accuracy of 96.93% and an F1-score of 95.79%. In addition to its predictive performance, the lightweight multimodal architecture substantially reduces computational complexity, inference latency, and carbon emissions, making it an energy-efficient solution for large-scale disease forecasting. The proposed framework provides a practical foundation for resource-efficient artificial intelligence in sustainable agriculture.

title: Travelling-Wave-Based Protection of DC Hubs in Bipolar HVDC Grids
summary: This paper presents a stationary wavelet transform (SWT)-based method for DC fault detection and classification in a three-terminal bipolar modular multilevel converter (MMC)-based HVDC system with a dedicated metallic return (DMR). The system incorporates DC switching stations (DCSSs) with interconnected DC circuit breakers (DCCBs). The method uses line-mode voltage wavelet detail energy for fault detection and wavelet detail energy derived from pole voltages and DMR current for fault classification, distinguishing pole-to-pole, pole-to-ground, and pole-to-DMR faults. Its performance is evaluated using a real-time hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) platform integrating an real-time digital simulator (RTDS) with embedded processing hardware. Busbar and cable faults with varying fault types, resistances, and locations are investigated. The results demonstrate the feasibility of real-time implementation and characterize the effects of fault location and travelling-wave propagation on transient energy and protection response time. The effectiveness of pole-voltage and DMR-current detail energy features in distinguishing fault types is also evaluated.

title: Doppler RaDAR Single-Frame Anomaly Detection and Consistency Assessment by Velocity-Conditioned Gaussian Spectral Modeling
summary: Reliable speed-over-ground estimation is essential for automated railway vehicles. However, the accuracy of a velocity estimate alone does not indicate whether the underlying RaDAR measurement is physically plausible. This paper introduces a velocity-conditioned Gaussian spectral modeling framework for anomaly detection and velocity consistency assessment. A neural encoder estimates the vehicle velocity from complex Doppler spectra, while a Gaussian decoder models the expected spectral distribution conditioned on a velocity estimate. Three complementary inference-time online indicators are derived: the spectral anomaly score (SAS), conditional anomaly score (CAS), and absolute velocity disagreement (AVD). Experiments demonstrate the sensitivity of the scores to velocity deviations. Under controlled spectral anomalies, SAS and CAS outperform conventional spectral indicators in most conditions. Furthermore, AVD exhibits strong correlations with actual velocity estimation errors (Pearson $r>0.99$) for the investigated extra-peak and local anomalies. These results demonstrate the potential of online conditional spectral modeling to assess measurement plausibility and velocity estimation reliability without requiring ground-truth velocities during inference.

title: On the Distance Properties of Huffman Sequences
comment: This work has been accepted to IEEE Signal Processing Letters
summary: In this letter, we study pairwise distances between sequences with a common aperiodic autocorrelation function. First, we show that pairwise distances are determined by a ternary signed pattern encoding the relative zero flips between spectral factors. Then, for Huffman sequences, we prove that Dihedral symmetries of the zeros preserve pairwise distances, and we further derive lower bounds on the minimum distance. The results in this letter offer a starting point for designing codes with a fixed autocorrelation. These codes are relevant in integrated sensing and communication.

title: Small Leaks Sink Great Ships: Automated Analysis of Protocols That Tolerate Low-Entropy Keys
comment: Accepted at NDSS 2027. 17 pages
summary: Modern cryptographic protocols such as WPA2-PSK, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), and Bluetooth Classic (BC) tolerate low-entropy keys for user-friendliness, backward compatibility, or resource-constrained deployment, yet existing symbolic protocol verifiers rely on the perfect-encryption assumption and therefore cannot reason about brute-force attackers. Prior work addresses this gap only through protocol-specific, manually encoded reveal rules, which neither generalize across protocols nor systematically explore compound-key decomposition. We introduce the first protocol-agnostic, automated symbolic methodology for low-entropy keys, built on three abstractions: the message-derivation fact MDerive, which captures brute-force prerequisites independently of concrete function symbols; a three-tier breaking-oracle design (value-breaking, relationship-breaking, message-derivation) that composes with the standard Dolev-Yao attacker; and a graded bit-level attacker model that bounds the key length an attacker is allowed to exhaust. We realize the methodology as EntropyVerif, a syntax-sugar extension of Tamarin that requires no kernel modification. Using EntropyVerif we automatically rediscover the PMKID, KNOB, and Method Confusion attacks, and uncover a new attack on BC which we call the Unilateral Multi-Downgrade (UMD) attack: by repeatedly downgrading one side of a BC session and recombining the recovered key fragments, an attacker reduces session-key recovery against devices using the maximum 128-bit key from $2^{128}$ to $n \cdot 2^{128/n}$, bottoming out at $2^{12}$ for $n=16$---a factor of $2^{116}$ reduction that has been responsibly disclosed to the Bluetooth SIG. Across three real-world protocols and six BC device configurations, our results show that entropy-aware symbolic analysis is both feasible and necessary.

title: Sequential Testing on Complex and High Dimensional Data Streams Leveraging Unsupervised Model Errors
comment: Preprint, 40 pages, 16 figures
summary: We propose two general, distribution-free test statistics for binary Sequential Hypothesis Testing (SHT) and Sequential Change Point Detection (SCPD) respectively, in streaming environments where the data (e.g., network traffic metadata) are too complicated for the exact probabilistic modeling required by conventional likelihood ratio-driven tests. Our framework also addresses the challenge of information asymmetry, where data is available only from the null/pre-change regime and not from the alternative/post-change one such as zero-day attacks or emerging disease related regimes. The proposed statistics monitor the errors of a predictive or reconstructive machine learning model trained solely on null/pre-change data, relying on imperfect generalization (the model's performance will degrade when deployed on data from the alternative/post-change class). Under mild assumptions on the model's errors, we establish rigorous analytical guarantees: strict non-asymptotic error control for SHT, and explicit bounds on the Average Run Length (ARL) and the Expected Detection Delay (EDD) for SCPD. Extensive evaluations in target tracking, chaotic dynamical systems, and real-world network security datasets, demonstrate that our framework consistently satisfies prescribed constraints where existing algorithms succumb to inflated missed detections and/or false alarms. Finally, because our methods operate on scalar errors without requiring online retraining or kernel evaluations, they are highly scalable.

title: Decentralized Control Barrier Function Filters for Frequency Containment With Inverters
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures
summary: This paper addresses the design of safety filters for grid-following (GFL) inverters in power transmission systems. The goal of the filters is to constrain frequency nadir and zenith following generation-demand imbalances, by supplementing primary frequency control. Using a reduced electromechanical model and control barrier functions (CBFs), we define an ideal filter through a convex quadratic program (QP). The ideal QP filter renders the set of admissible frequencies forward invariant; however, its direct implementation is impractical, as it requires centralized implementation and model-based computation. We then use a dual proximal formulation and a two-time-scale implementation to obtain decentralized dynamic filters that can be implemented at each inverter and use only local frequency and rate-of-change-of-frequency estimates. To assess the performance and the ability to regulate frequency, we derive bounds on the distance between state trajectories under the dynamic and ideal CBF filters. The bounds quantify the effects of the filter time constant, initialization, load variation, and frequency estimation errors, and provide estimates of possible frequency-limit violations. We validate the proposed method on the IEEE 39-bus system using a high-fidelity electromagnetic-transient (EMT) model.

title: First Order Real Resonant Digital Filters and A Novel Orthogonal State Generator
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures
summary: We describe FOREST, a real, first order digital resonant filter and orthogonal state generator. We show that in spite of the imaginary nature of the roots of the transfer function of a resonator, appropriate interpretation of this transfer function nonetheless leads to a practical first order filter with real coefficients. We use a discrete state space model of FOREST to predict the resonator properties, and implement the filter in digital signal processing slices on a digital signal processing platform. Applications are in real time digital signal processing, engineering fields such as mains electricity monitoring and motor control, any application requiring a phase locked loop, and physics applications utilising high-quality-factor resonators.

title: Simulation-Assisted Radio Map Reconstruction with Sparse Field Measurements
summary: Field measurements are essential for evaluating radio map reconstruction under real-world conditions, but their acquisition is costly. This letter proposes a simulation-assisted parameterized-background data-weak (SA-PBDW) method that combines propagation simulations with sparse field measurements, which jointly estimates background coefficients and a spatial correction to account for discrepancies between simulated and measured power distributions. Dense field measurements are collected for multiple transmitter positions at an urban site. Evaluations on the collected data and RadioMapSeer demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and structural fidelity over benchmark methods at reduced sampling rates.

title: The Detour Is the Danger: Preserving Security During LLM Agent Recovery
summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools and reusable Skills to execute complex workflows, autonomously replanning when operations fail. However, such recovery may preserve task functionality while silently discarding the security protections required by the original workflow. In this paper, we investigate workflow security downgrade, a failure-induced security threat in which agents execute sensitive operations without satisfying their original protection requirements. Unlike prompt injection, this threat exploits autonomous recovery decisions triggered by execution failures, without modifying instructions or tool definitions. We systematically evaluate this behavior through fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment spanning seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. To address this threat, we propose ARGUS, an obligation-preserving recovery framework that combines resource-bound security evidence, isolated recovery-plan validation, and execution-time enforcement. In a separate 864-run evaluation, ARGUS prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement, while recovery assistance yields model-dependent improvements in protected task completion over blocking alone. Our findings demonstrate that secure agent recovery requires preserving security obligations across workflow changes, rather than merely restoring task functionality.

title: Typical Angina, Reversed: A Long-Standing Documentation Error in the UCI Heart Disease Data
comment: 12 pages. Code and data: https://github.com/tpattabhi/anginaflip . An earlier version is on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24358545
summary:
The UCI Heart Disease data are a widely used machine-learning benchmark. We show that their chest-pain variable is stored in reverse of its documentation. At all four sites, the code documented as "asymptomatic" (4) marks patients with typical angina, and the code documented as "typical angina" (1) marks patients with almost none of the classical angina features (at Cleveland, no chest pain).
  Two complementary checks establish this: (i) the chest-pain table and regression coefficients of the original 1986 Cleveland study are reproduced only under the corrected reading; (ii) in the Budapest, Switzerland and Long Beach files, 93-96% of patients coded 4 have all three classical angina features. A 1990 word-labeled Cleveland file already uses the documented labels, and Statlog (Heart), a Cleveland subset, stores the same codes. OpenML, PMLB and two highly voted Kaggle copies that name the categories use the same documented labels (about 400,000 downloads combined).
  We audited a seeded random sample of 150 records from a pre-specified Scholar query for SHAP studies of these data mentioning asymptomatic chest pain (124 readable). Of 32 papers that state a direction for a named category, 25 (78%; 95% CI 61-89%) state one inconsistent with the corrected category identities; 22 (69%; 51-82%; post hoc) are attributable to the documentation error, and nine of these explain it clinically. None of the 124 readable papers identifies the reversal.
  Conventional models are essentially unaffected, one reason the error went unnoticed. Interpretations that attach the documented names to model effects are reversed, and zero-shot language-model classifiers that read the labels are misled: with the documented labels, three open-weight models lose 0.12-0.33 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) given age, sex and chest-pain type. We give the corrected mapping, evidence and code.

title: Grey-Box Experimental Identification of Reduced-Order Models for Grid-Forming Converters
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE TIE
summary: This paper proposes a grey-box system identification for identifying and validating reduced-order models (ROMs) of grid-forming (GFM) converters. Three reduced-order modeling techniques are compared within a common identification procedure: singular perturbation with frequency cutoff and participation factors (SP-PF), singular perturbation with energy residuals (SP-Energy), and balanced truncation (BT). Testing is on experimental data with real-life components. Results show that BT achieves the highest time-domain fit, followed by SP-Energy and SP-PF; SP-Energy better preserves key properties of the identified full-order model; BT places the dominant mode closest to the stability boundary and exhibits the highest sensitivity to parameter variations; SP-Energy outperforms SP-PF in both fit quality and consistency of modal preservation. Findings suggest that the model with the best time-domain fit does not always provide the most reliable representation of the modal properties for small-signal stability, with SP-Energy offering the best compromise between accuracy, physical interpretability, and modal preservation for the considered case study.

title: Device-Referred Channel Sounding With Commodity Wi-Fi Receivers: Error Budget and Body-Worn Measurements at 5 and 6 GHz
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation (Communication). Companion letter submitted to IEEE Antennas and Wireless Propagation Letters
summary: A wireless product experiences the channel through its own antennas and, when worn, its user's body. Commodity Wi-Fi receivers report channel state information (CSI) per frame and can serve as device-referred sounders if their impairments are corrected. Synthetic ground truth reproducing a commercial receiver's impairments shows that five corrections are needed: subcarrier mapping, receive-chain order, per-packet alignment, received-signal-strength referencing, and window-response removal. Without them, the RMS delay spread reads up to 191% high, the coherence bandwidth falls to about half, or the Rician $K$-factor and Doppler estimates lose their meaning; with all five, the median delay-spread bias is between $-6\%$ and $+14\%$. Applied to beacons from seven access points, including a body-worn receiver at six indoor sites at 5 and 6 GHz, the chain gives delay spreads of 24-96 ns; walking lowers the median correlation over one beacon interval from 0.85 to 0.15, near the estimator's floor. Unprecoded data frames gave 0.2-1.2 times the beacons' delay spread on the same channel, so the two should not be pooled.

title: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed-Solomon Codes
comment: 32 pages
summary: Linearized Reed-Solomon codes (LRS) are optimal sum-rank-metric codes that generalize both Reed-Solomon and Gabidulin codes, and benefit from excellent decoding capabilities, making them potentially interesting candidates for post-quantum code-based cryptography. Previous works have investigated the underlying geometric structure of LRS codes, identifying geometric invariants that distinguish them from random codes. Other works have proposed approaches to recovering the LRS structure from an arbitrary generator matrix, together with additional data. However, both the distinguishers and the recovery techniques proposed so far are either not fully general, or have a prohibitive computational complexity. In this paper, we propose a polynomial-time procedure for the full structure recovery of LRS codes from the sole knowledge of an arbitrary generator matrix. Our results show that, like their Hamming and rank metric counterparts, LRS codes cannot be used as they are for McEliece-like encryption. Our approach combines Overbeck-type attacks with suitable matrix manipulations and shortening techniques to recover the evaluation parameters across different ranges of code dimensions.

title: Bounding the security of the FALCON signature scheme in the quantum random oracle model
comment: 28 pages, submitted to PQCrypto 2027
summary: In 2016, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) announced their invitation for proposals of public key encryption and signature schemes that are resistant to attacks by quantum computers. Since then, several rounds of proposals and revisions have occurred resulting in the 2022 announcement that three signature schemes - CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FALCON, and SPHINCS+ - would be standardized. However, in 2024, work by Fouque et al. noted an oversight in the published security for FALCON, which they were only able to remedy in a classical computing setting, namely the random oracle model (ROM). In this paper, we provide the first complete security proof for FALCON in the quantum random oracle model (QROM). Specifically, we will prove a reduction to the security of FALCON from the ring inhomogeneous short integer solution (RISIS) problem and the NTRU learning problem utilizing known quantum reprogramming results. We then provide parameter sets which meet the security levels required by NIST under our reduction.

title: FERRETS: A Scalable Symbolic Transform for Time Series Classification
comment: 42 pages including references and appendices, 19 figures
summary: Dictionary methods for time series build bags of symbolic words from subsequences, but the accurate ones scale poorly. Against other families of methods, their accuracy no longer pays for their cost. We present FERRETS, a label-free dictionary transform built on WEASEL~2. It keys windows of random length and dilation into exact eight-bit words, adds a level word of each window's mean and spread, and on multivariate data adds cross-channel words. We compare it with leading classifiers, deep networks and foundation models included, on the UCR, Multiverse and MONSTER archives. FERRETS is the fastest of the eleven methods timed on UCR under a ten-thread budget. Of the ten others, only MultiRocket-Hydra is significantly more accurate, taking 24.7 times as long. FERRETS is not significantly different from WEASEL~2, the most accurate earlier dictionary method, which takes 125 times as long, and is significantly ahead of the other dictionary methods. On the Multiverse core, it is not significantly different in accuracy from HIVE-COTE~2 and MultiRocket-Hydra, though behind both on UCR. It is also significantly more accurate than five frozen foundation models on UCR's published split. On the MONSTER problems both complete, MiniRocket takes 3.7 times as long to fit as the streaming FERRETS classifier, which is significantly more accurate.

title: Gaussian Processes for Optimal Space-Filling Input Design
comment: Manuscript is under review at Automatica
summary: The quality of a model resulting from (black-box) system identification is highly dependent on the quality of the data that is used during the identification procedure. As nonlinear system identification is sensitive to modeling and extrapolation errors, having experiments that explore the considered operation range of interest are of high importance. The Gaussian-Process based space-filling input design strategy introduces an experiment design technique that aims to achieve a space-filling distribution within the argument space of a (nonlinear) approximator used for modeling the true system. Experiments carried out on simulation examples show that models trained with space-filling signals generalize better over the region of interest compared to models obtained from non-space-filling experiments. Moreover, the method is connected to the optimality theory of experiment design (V- and D-optimal design), allowing the experimenter to tailor the designed space-filling signal to maximize its information content with respect to the experiment objective.

title: Certified Outage Bounds for RIS-Assisted NOMA with Source-Side Thermal Energy Harvesting
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Submitted to IEEE Wireless Communications Letters. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24450534
summary: Gaussian useful-gain and mean-interference approximations can cause opposite power-sizing errors in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). We extend a source-side thermal energy harvesting model with Poisson interference and certify two-sided outage bounds. In a tested environment, the combined required signal-to-noise ratio error has opposite signs at 20 and 24 elements per user. Under another power convention, mean or moment-matched Gamma-distributed interference can predict false feasibility with exact useful gain. In the Gamma case, the Gaussian gain approximation can mask this false feasibility. Propagated Chernoff bounds give sufficient designs. Results concern the specified model and tested regimes.

title: Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections
comment: 41 pages
summary:
Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee.
  In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph.
  Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs.
  Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.

title: One Token, Many Lessons: Sliding-Window Attention within Gated Delta Networks
summary: Linear attention compresses historical context into a fixed-size recurrent state, reducing the computational and memory costs of long-sequence modeling. From the perspective of test-time regression (TTR), the state matrix can be viewed as an online-learned regression model, where keys and values serve as inputs and targets respectively, and queries are used to read from the model. From this perspective, the effectiveness of state learning depends not only on the update rule but also on how the key-value learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. While existing work has largely focused on how the state is updated and organized, we investigate how the learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. To this end, we propose Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (SWGDN), which replaces short convolutions in Delta-Rule linear attention with sliding-window attention to perform content-dependent local aggregation of projected queries, keys, and values. Our experiments show that SWGDN makes the key-value pairs used in consecutive updates more similar in both GDN2 and KDA. In SWGDN, carrying information from the same token across updates can help the recurrent state reinforce a previously learned association. The local mixing strategy can be incorporated into any Delta-Rule-based linear attention architecture without changing its state update equations or chunkwise parallel algorithms. We apply this strategy to two Delta-Rule variants, GDN2 and KDA, and experimental results demonstrate that SWGDN outperforms the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.

title: Azimuth Pointing and Momentum Management for a Lightweight High-Altitude Balloon Payload
comment: Accepted to the 2027 IEEE Aerospace Conference
summary: The ALTAIR (Airborne Laser for Telescopic Atmospheric Interference Reduction) project provides photometric calibration for ground-based telescopes by flying an integrating sphere as an artificial star-like calibration source on a high-altitude balloon. Because the angular distribution of light from the exit port of the sphere is approximately Lambertian, the payload must keep its azimuth within $\pm8^\circ$ of the telescope line of sight. This condition bounds the fractional difference in light intensity from that along the exit-port normal to below 1%. The bound must be held for at least 30 s at a time. This paper presents a pointing architecture that combines passive stabilization, onboard attitude determination, and active azimuth control using a momentum wheel, with active desaturation through a second motor at the flight-train pivot. Carbon-fiber inertial booms reduce off-axis pendulating motion sufficiently for azimuth control to be treated independently. Attitude is determined by onboard fusion of rate gyro, accelerometer, magnetometer, and dual-antenna GNSS carrier-phase measurements. A high-fidelity simulation of the payload, including motor dynamics and limits, sensor noise, and wind disturbances generated from flight data, is used to size actuators and tune the control loops. The payload avionics, flight software, power management, controls, and real-time ground telemetry systems are developed in-house. The system is evaluated through ground testing, simulation, and two flights. With the momentum wheel alone, 53 intervals of 30 s pointing within $\pm8^\circ$ of the target azimuth are recorded during ascent, with a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of $3.7^\circ$, and the longest uninterrupted window lasts 7 min 55 s with $5^\circ$ of pointing RMSE. Simulation results suggest significant performance improvements from adding a pivot motor for momentum management.

title: AutoRSP: An AI Agent for Radar Sensing Pipeline Design
summary: Radar sensing demands a pipeline that is well-thought-out across hardware and software. We ask whether an AI agent can automatically design radar sensing pipelines at a fraction of the time, cost, and expertise that current practice needs. We present AutoRSP, an agent that embeds radar-system-level structure through sub-agents mapped to five stack layers, a code-based representation of every layer with explicitly modeled cross-layer dependencies. Feedback for the agentic search process comes from a pipeline of realistic RF simulation, on-sensor emulation, and execution on real edge devices, rather than from an LLM judge. Because such feedback can be slower than an LLM call, we present methods to efficiently optimize agentic loops. We evaluate AutoRSP on robotic imaging, automotive perception, and vital sign sensing. It produces executable pipelines with performance comparable to or better than human-expert pipelines and closed-source agents. AutoRSP's harness, tools, and benchmarks will be released to bridge the rising gap in agentic research abilities outside of frontier labs.

title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs
comment: 36 pages. Code, 11 specifications, 28 Lean 4 modules, Rust verifier, and GPU benchmark receipts: https://github.com/s-JoL/FlashProve-Next
summary:
Clients of closed-weight LLM APIs cannot verify whether a provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. Existing approaches either trust hardware or third parties, or re-prove every layer of an integer surrogate at high cost while diverging from native floating-point serving.
  FlashProve-Next produces verifiable, zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual LLM API responses without modifying native serving (bf16/fp8/mxfp4, random sampling, FlashAttention, CUDA graphs, batching, prefix caching) and without disclosing weights, hidden prompts, hidden reasoning, or activations (dense profiles fix coarse geometry; cross-architecture hiding is deferred). A non-depleting Reed-Solomon weight commitment model_id opens inside proofs via hidden column openings, while local per-operator rounding contracts remove integer surrogates and the refusal-bit leak. Cost-weighted spot-checking supports non-interactive public verification (NI-315, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-40}$, $Q \le 2^{64}$) and external-seed C_pre mode (ExtSeed-153, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-20}$, $Q_{\rm samp} \le 2^{30}$).
  Twenty-eight Lean 4 modules (696 declarations, zero sorry, standard axioms only) mechanize round-by-round soundness, bucketed sampling, $\mathbb{F}_{p^3}$ constrained-mask binding, causal masking, six IR gadgets, and executable FPN2 verifiers. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding $Q=128$, passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev $4+2$) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). Rust fpn-verify checks 8 MiB FPN2 Relation 2 proofs in 10.1 ms on CPU.

title: Fast and Scalable Abstract Interpretation for Deep Neural Networks
summary:
Abstract interpretation can certify properties of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), but precise analyses remain expensive. General implementations repeat work when analyzing the same architecture under different inputs and properties. Interleaving this work with numerical operations limits GPU utilization and restricts how much of the analysis a tensor compiler can process together.
  We present Scepter, a framework for specializing DNN abstract interpreters through structural semantics. The semantics determine the structure of intermediate abstract values while deferring their numerical evaluation. Structural computations from successive operations can therefore be performed together before certification, generating an executable tensor program. With the abstract interpreter and DNN architecture fixed, the program can be reused with different weights and input regions. We prove that it computes the same bounds as the general interpreter in exact arithmetic. The generated program also exposes operations and their dependencies for tensor compilation and memory planning. We implement Scepter for the tensor programs that Neuton generates from ConstraintFlow specifications.
  We evaluate Scepter on eight abstract interpreters and 44 DNNs against six baseline systems on GPUs and CPUs. Scepter handles networks with up to 153x as many neurons as the largest completed by the corresponding baselines. It completes DeepPoly on ResNet50 and VGG-16, whereas none of the evaluated DeepPoly baselines completes either network. On configurations completed by both systems, GPU geometric-mean speedups over Neuton range from 11.9x to 44.4x across eight analyses, with a 2.60x geometric-mean reduction in peak memory. In an input-splitting case study, Scepter proves 68 properties for which the baselines time out.
  Code: https://github.com/uiuc-focal-lab/constraintflow.git

title: Adaptive Control Barrier Functions for Nonlinear Singularly Perturbed Systems
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures
summary: Control barrier functions (CBFs) have emerged as a flexible and efficient approach for enforcing dynamic safety constraints. In this paper, we consider a class of uncertain nonlinear systems with singular perturbations and develop an adaptive CBF framework for such systems to enforce safety constraints on both the slow and fast subsystems in the overall singularly perturbed nonlinear system with uncertain parameters. We first develop a robustness property showing that if an adaptive controller for the slow subsystem satisfies the slow CBF condition with an appropriate safety margin, then for sufficiently small values of the singular perturbation parameter $\varepsilon$, the slow subsystem remains within an $O(\varepsilon)$-neighborhood of its safe set. We then consider the more general case of safety constraints on both the fast and slow subsystems and provide conditions under which joint slow-fast safety is achieved despite the parametric uncertainties. The reduced-order slow model and the slow and fast CBF conditions are evaluated using an online parameter estimate and the parameter mismatch between the estimated and true reduced-order models is addressed via a state-dependent robustness margin in the CBF inequalities. To illustrate the proposed framework, we present simulation studies for two systems with parametric uncertainties: a synthetic two-time-scale fourth-order example system and a unicycle with a fast turn-rate actuator and an obstacle avoidance safety constraint.

title: On the Distance Properties of Huffman Sequences
comment: This work has been accepted to IEEE Signal Processing Letters
summary: In this letter, we study pairwise distances between sequences with a common aperiodic autocorrelation function. First, we show that pairwise distances are determined by a ternary signed pattern encoding the relative zero flips between spectral factors. Then, for Huffman sequences, we prove that Dihedral symmetries of the zeros preserve pairwise distances, and we further derive lower bounds on the minimum distance. The results in this letter offer a starting point for designing codes with a fixed autocorrelation. These codes are relevant in integrated sensing and communication.

title: Agentic-Level Adversarial Purification: Revisiting Diffusion Purifiers on Native-Resolution Agentic Inputs
summary: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages, where one perturbed photo or a few altered text strokes can redirect the decision. Any content provider can craft such a perturbation on the open model behind the agent, so a plug-in purifier is the natural first line of defense. Yet diffusion purifiers were designed and evaluated at the fixed resolution of the diffusion model on classifier or natural-image benchmarks, and defense evaluations for agents test JPEG, blur and noise but no diffusion purifier. We present the first study of adversarial purification at the agentic level, for an agent built on Qwen3-VL-8B: purifiers run at native resolution on multi-element inputs, face grey-box attackers who know the agent's model but not the defense, and are compared at matched clean cost. We show that treating agentic inputs as classifier inputs misleads both evaluation and design. Resizing the input to the resolution of the diffusion model, as existing purifiers do, raises the TextVQA clean cost of the Divide-and-Conquer purifier (DC) from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages, DC keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy against web-hardened perturbations, where cheap input transformations at matched clean cost keep at most 40.0%, and this robustness comes from the global noise level: input-estimated masks and noise levels add none. These findings hold on a disjoint held-out set and on a second VLM and yield three requirements for defenses, we release the protocol.

title: Two Timescales of Forgetting in Fine-tuning of Language Models: Fast Behavioral Suppression and Slow Representational Drift
comment: 36 pages, 27 figures. Code: https://github.com/yilin-luo/two-timescales-of-forgetting
summary: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.

title: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code
summary: Language models can generate Python that drives industrial protocols on programmable logic controllers, yet existing code-grounding checks ask whether an imported package or symbol exists rather than whether it suits the declared industrial target. We define \emph{metadata-conditioned, import-level vendor--protocol incompatibility} and build \textsc{Proteus-OT}, a label-free static verifier over a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 180 carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target (20.4\%); restricting to single-vendor targets gives 16.3\%, and additionally requiring the offending library to reach a protocol communication call gives 14.2\%, which we read as conditional on the corpus metadata rather than on verified intent. None of the 28 adjudicable human control files carries one, a sample too small to estimate a prevalence. Within the balanced subset, 96.6\% of mismatching scripts import packages and call methods that exist, so an existence baseline does not represent them, and every positive ships with an inspectable witness. We also audit machine-versus-human classification on the same corpus, where character $n$-grams reach macro-F1 1.000 under task, model and vendor-disjoint partitions and survive comment removal, an AST round trip and identifier anonymisation. The trailing newline present in 95.2\% of human files and in none of the generated ones separates the classes on its own. Vendor--protocol consistency is a useful static audit target, whereas provenance classification on repository-labelled corpora is not authorship detection.

title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
summary: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.

title: Evaluating Post-Quantum and Hybrid Signatures for Blockchains: Performance, Storage and Ledger Growth
summary: Advances in quantum computing pose a long-term threat to blockchain systems that rely on classical digital signature schemes such as ECDSA. Migrating these systems to post-quantum cryptography introduces practical costs beyond cryptographic security, including larger transactions, higher computational costs and faster ledger growth. We present an empirical evaluation of 13 signature configurations in a common simulated blockchain framework: ECDSA, ML-DSA-44/65/87, Falcon-512/1024, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, and six hybrids combining ECDSA with each post-quantum scheme. We measure signing and verification costs, transaction-processing throughput, and signature and public-key sizes, and project the measured overheads onto five public blockchains: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, BNB Smart Chain and TRON. Verification remains inexpensive for the evaluated lattice-based schemes, with Falcon-512 achieving a verification time comparable to ECDSA (30.1 versus 32.8 $μ$s). Storage overheads, however, are substantial. Under our modelling assumptions, had the recorded transaction histories used Falcon-512, the most compact post-quantum scheme evaluated, ledger sizes would have been 79--229% larger, depending on the blockchain. Hybrid configurations introduce relatively modest additional storage overhead compared with their standalone post-quantum counterparts, while ECDSA+Falcon-512 approximately doubles the verification cost of standalone Falcon-512. Existing transaction- and script-size limits also present obstacles to straightforward migration in Bitcoin and Solana. Overall, our findings suggest that storage overhead may pose a greater challenge than signature verification costs when migrating blockchain systems to post-quantum cryptography.

title: Change Partners at Every Layer: Balanced Random Regrouping for Model Merging
comment: 26 pages, including appendix
summary: Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one model that serves many tasks without retraining, but merging many experts this way substantially reduces accuracy. Grouping offers a middle ground: at every layer or weight matrix, the $N$ experts are divided into $K<N$ groups, the experts in a group are merged into one shared module, and a task uses the module merged from its expert's group. Natural choices are to keep the same partners across layers or to group similar experts. Surprisingly, we find that randomly changing partners at every layer outperforms both. We call this Balanced Random Regrouping (BRR): it independently partitions the experts into $K$ equal-sized random groups at each layer (BRR-layer) or weight matrix (BRR-matrix) and merges each group with an existing method. With validation-selected merge scales, both BRR variants outperform reusing one grouping across layers in all 24 CLIP settings, by 1.0-6.8 points, and BRR-matrix also outperforms the similarity-based FlexMerge in every setting. A first-order analysis explains this gain. At each layer, merging a task's expert with its partners shifts the task's output features; when the partners are the same at every layer, these shifts tend to point in similar directions and add up, whereas with new partners at every layer they vary independently and add up less on average. A series of experiments supports this analysis, which further guides a grouping search that can outperform BRR.

title: Discovering Explicit Magnetic Core-Loss Equations via Symbolic Sparse Identification
summary: Compact core loss equations are essential tools in magnetic component design, but existing approaches trade accuracy against interpretability. Empirical models such as the Steinmetz Equation (SE) yield compact expressions of limited accuracy, while machine learning methods achieve high accuracy as black-box predictors. This paper bridges the gap with a Symbolic Sparse Identification (SSI) framework, which casts core loss modeling as a data-driven symbolic regression problem and recovers unknown equations directly from measured data, without presuming a functional form. First, a comprehensively expanded library of symbolic candidate terms far richer than the SE is constructed. Second, the governing terms are isolated from this library by sparse regression. Third, the coefficients of the retained terms are refined with an AdamW optimizer to maximize accuracy and form an analytical equation. Experiments on Fair-Rite 78, 79, and 95 yield test mean absolute percentage errors of 1.89%, 1.01%, and 1.56%, respectively, with only 10, 10, and 7 active terms. Comparisons with empirical, numerical, and symbolic models quantify the resulting balance of accuracy and compactness. SSI thus provides an explicit and physically guided approach for high-frequency magnetic characterization and design.

title: Latent-in-the-Middle: On the Security of Cross-Model Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
summary:
As large language models increasingly collaborate in heterogeneous multi-agent systems, latent communication has emerged as an efficient alternative to exchanging natural-language messages. By sharing internal representations, agents can avoid repeatedly processing the same context, reducing communication overhead and prefill computation. One such mechanism is cross-model Key-Value (KV) cache transfer, which uses a learned mapper to translate a source model's KV cache into one a target model can use. However, this handoff means the target model consumes context it did not encode itself, thus calling into question whether its safety alignment still holds.
  In this work, we investigate the security implications of latent handoffs by introducing Chasm, a framework characterizing cross-model handoff attacks across three new attack surfaces: the source model, mapper, and handoff mechanism itself. Our experiments reveal that latent handoffs substantially undermine safety alignment and prompt-injection defenses. Notably, a target model that follows only 0.4% of benchmark prompt injections natively, follows up to 44.2% when transferred through a mapper from a source model. On the other hand, for jailbreak attacks, transfer alone raises attack success by up to 24.6 pp within a model family and zero-shot attacks by up to 69.2 pp, whereas white-box optimization through the mapper boosts the attack success rate to 92.5%, against 37.5% for ordinary GCG on the same target. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose a lightweight target-side cache guard that corrects transferred caches to restore the target model's refusal, considerably mitigating these attacks.

title: Sparse Adaptation for In-Context Learning on Data Streams
summary: The Internet of Things (IoT) generates massive data streams, making edge computing essential for low-latency applications and 5G networks. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) enable adaptation through in-context examples rather than parameter updates, but evolving streams challenge context relevance and computational efficiency. This work introduces SAIL, a framework for sparse adaptation of TFMs that reuses the model's key--value cache between adaptation events. SAIL reconstructs its support set only when drifts in stream structure indicate potential context inadequacy, while the structural representation itself is updated by changes in predictive performance. SAIL combines prequential error monitoring with online, class-specific micro-clustering to detect changes in cluster mass, class separability, and feature-space coverage. Upon adaptation, a context budget is allocated proportionally to class mass, and the most recently updated micro-clusters provide representative observations for refitting. This limits context redundancy and computational cost while preserving recent structural information.

title: Robust Adaptive Channel Estimation for RIS-Assisted mmWave Massive MIMO via a Stochastic Shannon Entropy Criterion
summary: Accurate channel estimation in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems remains challenging due to the passive nature of the RIS, the high dimensionality of the cascaded channel, and the presence of non-Gaussian impulsive disturbances. This paper proposes a robust sparsity-aware adaptive estimator, termed reweighted zero-attracting stochastic Shannon entropy (RZA-SSE), for angular-domain channel estimation. The algorithm combines a double-window kernel-based Shannon entropy criterion with a norm-normalized \(\ell_1\) penalty. Both the data-driven term and the nonsmooth penalty are differentiated using exact Wirtinger calculus. An exact weight-error recursion and a mean-square energy relation are derived. Local stability is analyzed via a joint coefficient--penalty state representation, and an approximate steady-state mean-square deviation (MSD) expression is obtained. Extensive simulations under Gaussian-mixture impulsive noise demonstrate that ZA-SSE consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art benchmarks in steady-state MSD.

title: Poisoning Attacks to Local Differential Privacy Protocols for Dynamic Graphs
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, submitted to conference. Code available at https://github.com/spiralfood/GraphPoison-LDP
summary: With the increasing adoption of privacy-preserving techniques in dynamic graph analysis, local differential privacy (LDP) has become a fundamental paradigm for protecting user data in decentralized environments. However, despite its strong privacy guarantees, LDP-based dynamic graph protocols remain vulnerable to data poisoning attacks through malicious data injection. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of data poisoning attacks against privacy-preserving dynamic graphs under the LDP framework. Considering the temporal evolution of dynamic graphs, we identify key challenges in attack design and evaluation, including how to schedule attack resources across time and how to measure cumulative attack impact. To address these challenges, we introduce an absolute gain metric to quantify the overall deviation of graph statistical metrics before and after attacks across time. Based on this metric, we further propose a unified poisoning attack framework for dynamic graphs, which consists of target node selection, dynamic fake node scale scheduling, and fake edge injection. Within this framework, we design a temporal enhanced attack (TEA) strategy that dynamically schedules attack resources to maximize attack effectiveness, along with two baseline strategies, equal-scale attack (ESA) and random-scale attack (RSA), for comparison. Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed attacks can significantly degrade the accuracy of graph metric estimation for target nodes.

title: Online Prediction System for Proactive Autoscaling
summary: We present an online learning system for short-term time series forecasting that enables proactive autoscaling in large-scale distributed systems. Unlike traditional forecasting methods that focus on modeling seasonality and long-term trends, the system targets high-accuracy, low-latency predictions for immediate future intervals for dynamic resource management in internet-scale infrastructures. The system employs a two-stage architecture: a seasonality decomposition stage followed by a residual correction stage using lightweight linear models with engineered features. By retraining models on-the-fly for every prediction cycle, the online prediction system continuously adapts to changing demand patterns without requiring persistent model storage or feature drift monitoring. Deployed across many heterogeneous services, the system processes over 900K predictions per hour; in an offline evaluation on production traffic, its STL-based configuration reduces prediction error (MAPE) by 18.6\% relative to the previous production model. In production, the system has saved an estimated 118K servers daily.

title: SOC-Net: Second-Order-Cone-Constrained Neural Networks
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: In many applications, neural networks must learn input-output maps that respect prior knowledge such as physical laws, safety requirements, and operating limits. These requirements constrain which outputs are admissible for a given input and often admit second-order cone (SOC) representations, including norm bounds and robust linear inequalities. Examples in control include friction cones, thrust bounds, and input-robust control barrier function (CBF) conditions. However, existing approaches to enforcing general input-dependent SOC constraints require a conic solver, an iterative scheme whose feasibility depends on convergence, or an interior feasible point for each input. We propose SOC-Net, a neural network architecture that enforces input-dependent SOC constraints by construction for every input, even outside the training distribution. SOC-Net projects an affine lifting of the backbone output onto the reachable slice of a fixed product of Lorentz cones and maps the correction back to the output space. For separable constraints, this projection splits into one projection per cone, and each is available in closed form or reduces to a single scalar equation, regardless of the cone dimension. We prove that SOC-Net retains the expressive power of the backbone network under regularity conditions and accommodates end-to-end training by standard backpropagation with an explicit Jacobian. Experiments on contact force allocation with friction constraints and 3-D obstacle avoidance with an input-robust CBF demonstrate that SOC-Net satisfies the constraints at every evaluated input, with lower evaluation latency than the tested solver-based and iterative baselines.

title: AgentLens: Graph-guided Security Auditing for LLM-based Agents
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: LLM-based agents are emerging as a key paradigm for automating software engineering by coupling LLM-driven decision-making with external tools, files, APIs, and execution environments. However, weaknesses in agent implementations and insecure interactions between the agent and external resources can lead to severe consequences, including remote code execution, arbitrary file access, SQL injection, and data leakage.
